Deployment Guide

What are we building?

We create an HTML page and deploy it on AWS, so anyone can open it in a browser. That is the end goal.

Private values (names, emails, account IDs, card details, repository and project names) are shown as **** or <placeholders>

What we need

Everything below is created once; the page itself is the only thing that changes from release to release.

AWS account

Owns and pays for everything. This setup has three accounts; the site lives in the workload one.

Terraform

Builds every AWS piece below from code with one terraform apply, and can remove them all again with one destroy. No clicking around the console.

S3 bucket (website)

Private storage that holds index.html. Nobody reads it directly.

CloudFront

Gives the page its public HTTPS address and serves it fast worldwide.

S3 bucket (Terraform state)

Terraform's memory of what it built, kept safe in AWS.

GitHub repository + Actions

Holds the code and the page; a workflow uploads the page to AWS with one click.

IAM role + OIDC

Lets GitHub sign in to AWS with short-lived access, so no AWS keys are stored in GitHub.

Health check, alarm, email

Route 53 checks the page every 30 s; CloudWatch raises an alarm; SNS emails you.

AWS CLI

Installed on your PC; signs you in to AWS so Terraform and the setup script can work.

App architecture: serve and watch

What happens after the page is deployed, for every visitor and every health check. This is lanes 3 (Visit) and 4 (Monitor) of the data flow, in more detail.

Serve: one page view

  1. The browser opens https://d****.cloudfront.net. Plain http:// is redirected to https://.
  2. CloudFront has caching turned off, so it asks the bucket each time, signing the request with its origin access control (OAC).
  3. S3 checks its bucket policy: only this CloudFront distribution may read, and only over HTTPS. It returns index.html.
  4. CloudFront adds security headers and sends the page back with status 200.
  5. Anyone who opens the bucket's own URL gets 403 Forbidden.

Watch: the health check

  1. Route 53 health checkers in several AWS locations load the page over HTTPS every 30 seconds, through CloudFront like a visitor.
  2. A check passes when the page answers and contains the page title text. After 3 failures in a row the check counts as unhealthy.
  3. The result becomes the CloudWatch metric HealthCheckStatus: 1 healthy, 0 unhealthy.
  4. The alarm looks at the lowest value each minute. Below 1 for 2 minutes in a row, or no data at all, means ALARM.
  5. Each change of state goes to the SNS topic, which emails alert_email: ALARM when the site breaks, OK when it recovers.

Infrastructure architecture: build, deploy, serve, watch

The app has four parts. Each number in the picture is explained underneath.

BUILDTerraform on your PC creates all the AWS pieces and remembers them in the state bucket.
DEPLOYGitHub signs in to AWS without keys and uploads the page.
SERVECloudFront gives the page a public HTTPS address and reads it from a private bucket.
WATCHRoute 53 checks the page, CloudWatch raises an alarm, SNS emails you.

What each piece does

#PieceWhat it isWhat it does in this app
1Your PCTerraform + AWS CLIYou run terraform apply here once; it creates pieces 2, 4, 5, 6, 8, 9 and 10 in AWS. The AWS CLI is how Terraform signs in.
2State bucketAmazon S3 (storage)Terraform's memory: a file listing everything it built, so the next run knows what already exists. Private, versioned, encrypted.
3GitHubRepository + GitHub ActionsHolds the code and index.html. The Deploy website workflow uploads the page when you click Run workflow.
4IAM deploy roleAWS IAM, trusting GitHub through OIDCThe badge GitHub wears in AWS. GitHub proves who it is with a signed token; AWS (STS) hands it short-lived access. It may only upload index.html, so no AWS keys are stored in GitHub.
5Website bucketAmazon S3 (storage)Stores index.html. Completely private: nobody can open it directly, only CloudFront. Keeps old versions, encrypts files.
6CloudFrontAmazon CloudFront (content delivery network)The public front door: gives the page its https://d****.cloudfront.net address, forces HTTPS, adds security headers, and fetches the page from the bucket with its own key (OAC). Caching is off, so a new upload shows at once.
7VisitorsAny web browserOpen the CloudFront address and see the page.
8Route 53 health checkAmazon Route 53A robot visitor: every 30 s it loads the page over HTTPS from several places and checks the page title is there. (Only its health check is used; there is no custom domain.)
9CloudWatch alarmAmazon CloudWatch (monitoring)Watches the health-check result. If the page fails for 2 minutes it switches to ALARM; when the page recovers it switches back to OK.
10SNS topicAmazon SNS (notifications)The messenger: when the alarm changes state it sends a message to everyone subscribed.
11Your emailThe address in alert_emailReceives the ALARM and OK messages, once you have confirmed the subscription.

Only CloudFront can read the website bucket. GitHub can only upload index.html, and only from this repository's staging environment.

How to read this guide

Every section answers the same questions: what it does, why it is needed, how to do it, and what you will see when it worked.

ONE TIME · check before redoing EVERY RELEASE MANUAL AUTOMATED Management account Workload account GitHub Your PC

One-time steps have an orange Check first box: if the check passes, skip the step. Placeholders: <owner>/<repo> = your GitHub account and repository, <project> = the name prefix in terraform/site/main.tf, <account-id> = a 12-digit AWS account number.

1 · Prerequisites

1aTools and your AWS user ONE TIMEYour PCWorkload account

WHATInstall the AWS CLI and Terraform, create an IAM user with an access key, and point the CLI at it.
WHYEvery later command (the script, Terraform) runs on your PC and needs to sign in to AWS as you.
YOU'LL SEEBoth tools print a version, and aws sts get-caller-identity shows the workload account.
Check first: in a new Command Prompt run the three commands below. If both tools answer and the account is the workload account, skip to the next section. 
aws --version
terraform --version          # 1.10 or later, below 2.0
aws sts get-caller-identity  # "Account" must be the workload account

A1 · AWS CLI and IAM user (V0 steps 1 to 4)

  1. Install the AWS CLI from aws.amazon.com/cli/, open a new Command Prompt, run aws --version.
  2. Use your AWS account (this setup has three, see the next section). Set a budget and alerts; turn on MFA for the root user.
  3. In the workload account: IAM › Users › Create user.
  4. Attach policies directly › AdministratorAccess › create. Study accounts only; remove it after the lab.

A2 · Access key and aws configure (V0 steps 5 to 7)

  1. IAM › Users › your user › Security credentials › Create access key › Command Line Interface (CLI). The secret is shown once; save it privately.
  2. Run aws configure: your key, your secret, region us-east-1, output json.
  3. Run aws sts get-caller-identity and check Account and Arn.
Never share, commit, paste into chat or AI tools, or screenshot access keys.

A3 · Terraform (V0 steps 8 to 11)

  1. Download the Windows ZIP from developer.hashicorp.com/terraform/install, extract terraform.exe to e.g. C:\Tools\Terraform.
  2. Windows search › Edit environment variables for your account › Path › Edit › New › that folder › OK. Reopen Command Prompt.
  3. terraform --version must be 1.10 or later, below 2.0.

1bThe three AWS accounts

WHATAWS's account setup created an organization with three accounts, each with one job.
WHYA mistake in the account that runs projects cannot touch billing, the organization's rules, or who can sign in.
YOU'LL SEEOne card per account on the AWS sign-ins page. The account you are in shows at the top right of every console page.

Management account

The owner's office. Owns the organization, pays one combined bill, holds the credits and the rules (SCPs). Open it only for billing and rules.

Identity delegated admin

The security desk. Runs IAM Identity Center, which gives you the AccountFullAccessRole sign-in. Nothing to do here.

Workload account

The workshop. Everything this project builds lives here (named First Principles in this setup). The CLI and GitHub use it.

  1. Open https://console.aws.amazon.com/: the AWS sign-ins page lists one card per account.
  2. Select the account name (already signed in) or Sign in. This only opens a session; it changes nothing.
2 · One-time manual setup

Why these steps are manual

These are done once and are deliberately left to a person: they involve money, AWS's own approval, organization-wide security rules, or settings shared with other projects.

StepWhy a person does itWhere
Payment methodCard details must only ever be typed by you on AWS's own page.Management
CreditsJust a look, to know what is covered.Management
CloudFront verificationAWS Support decides; no command can lift the hold.Workload
Region rule (SCP)It guards every account, lives in the management account, and the workload CLI user cannot change it. Each change should be a conscious decision.Management
GitHub login providerOne per account, shared by every project; created once and then reused.Workload

2aPayment method ONE TIMEMANUALManagement account

WHATA credit card on the management account.
WHYIt pays for all three accounts. Credits are used first; the card only pays what they do not cover.
YOU'LL SEEThe card (last digits) under Default payment preferences.
Check first: Billing and Cost Management › Payment preferences. A card already listed under Payment method? Skip.
  1. Sign in to the management account, search Billing, open Billing and Cost Management.
  2. Left menu Payments › Payment preferences › Add payment method.
  3. Type the card yourself on AWS's page and make it the default.
Never put card numbers, security codes, passwords or MFA codes into chat, AI tools, files or screenshots.

2bCredits and free tier ONE TIME lookManagement account

WHAT$120 of credits: $100 AWS Free Tier + $20 for setting up a budget, valid to 11/23/2027.
WHYThey cover Route 53, CloudFront, S3, CloudWatch and SNS: everything this site uses.
YOU'LL SEEBilling › Credits: amount used and remaining (updated about once a day).

2cCloudFront account verification ONE TIMEMANUALWorkload account

WHATA free AWS Support case asking AWS to verify the account.
WHYNew accounts fail with "Your account must be verified before you can add new CloudFront resources". Only AWS can lift it.
YOU'LL SEEThe case changes to Resolved (ours took a few hours).
Check first: Support Center › Support Cases. Already Resolved, or no such error on apply? Skip.
  1. Workload account: search Support, or open https://console.aws.amazon.com/support/home.
  2. In Describe your issue, explain you need CloudFront and paste the error. Then Create a case.
  3. Account and billing › Account Activation › Account Verification › severity General question. Submit.
  4. Wait for Resolved before terraform apply.

2dRegion rule (SCP) ONE TIMEMANUALManagement account

WHATAllow S3, SNS and the CloudWatch alarm actions in us-east-1 in the organization's region policy.
WHYThe policy allows only global services in us-east-1, but the health-check alarm must live there. Our first apply failed with "explicit deny in a service control policy".
YOU'LL SEEThe new entries in the policy's Content; then terraform apply no longer fails on SNS, S3 or the alarm.

What each region allows (this is why "some services don't work")

RegionAllowed
us-east-2 (Ohio)Everything.
us-east-1 (N. Virginia)Only the exempted list: global services (IAM, CloudFront, Route 53, ACM, STS, billing, support...) plus S3, SNS and the alarm actions we added. EC2 instances, Lambda, DynamoDB and others are denied.
us-west-2 (Oregon)A short list: Bedrock model calls, CloudShell, KMS decrypt, Identity Center, Health, Service Quotas, Support, Trusted Advisor.
All other regionsDenied, except Bedrock model calls.
Four BudgetsSpendLimit… SCPs (Bedrock, Lambda, SageMaker, new chargeable resources) are managed by AWS Budgets and block those services only when forecast spend nears your limit. They are not applied to the workload account today.
Check first: open the policy's Content and search (Ctrl+F) for "sns:*" and "s3:*". Both there, plus the four cloudwatch: actions below? Skip.
  1. Management account: AWS Organizations › Policies › Service control policies › AdvancedModeRegionRestrictionSecurityControlPolicy (Targets: Root).
  2. Content: find "Sid": "UsEast1Partitional". Its NotAction list is what is allowed in us-east-1.
  3. Back up the whole JSON to a local file first (SCPs keep no history).
  4. Edit policy, in that list only: replace the "s3:..." entries with "s3:*"; add "sns:*", "cloudwatch:PutMetricAlarm", "cloudwatch:DeleteAlarms", "cloudwatch:TagResource", "cloudwatch:UntagResource".
  5. Save changes (warnings on entries that were already there do not block saving), reload, confirm. Applies at once to every account.
More screenshots: policy content top, and what applies to the workload account

2eGitHub login provider (OIDC) ONE TIMEMANUALWorkload account

WHATRegister GitHub as a trusted sign-in source in IAM.
WHYGitHub Actions can then get short-lived AWS access, so no AWS keys are ever stored in GitHub.
YOU'LL SEEtoken.actions.githubusercontent.com with audience sts.amazonaws.com, and its ARN.
Check first: IAM › Identity providers. Listed already? Reuse it and copy its ARN (only one per account).
  1. Workload account: IAM › Access management › Identity providers.
  2. If missing: Add provider › OpenID Connect, URL https://token.actions.githubusercontent.com, audience sts.amazonaws.com.
  3. Copy the ARN arn:aws:iam::<account-id>:oidc-provider/token.actions.githubusercontent.com (not the deploy role ARN).
3 · Automated setup

What is automated, and how

ToolWhat it does for youYou run
scripts\bootstrap-state.ps1Creates or checks the Terraform state bucket and backend.hcl.1 command, once per environment
Terraform (terraform/site)Builds, changes or removes all 15 AWS resources of the site.init, plan, apply, output
GitHub Actions ChecksChecks Terraform format and validity on every push to main. Never touches AWS.Nothing (automatic)
GitHub Actions Deploy websiteSigns in to AWS, uploads web/index.html, checks the live page matches.1 click per release

3State bucket: one command ONE TIMEAUTOMATEDYour PC

WHATA private, versioned, encrypted, HTTPS-only S3 bucket for Terraform's state, plus backend.hcl that points Terraform at it.
WHYThe state is Terraform's memory of what it built. It must survive your PC and every destroy.
YOU'LL SEECreated and verified state bucket the first time, or all [OK] and Nothing was changed after that.

What the script does in each situation

It findsIt doesAsks?
CLI signed in to another accountStops, no changeNo
No backend.hclCreates the bucket, turns on block public access, versioning, AES256 encryption, adds the HTTPS-only policy, verifies all, writes backend.hclYes, once
backend.hcl, bucket fully set upAll [OK], Nothing was changedNo
backend.hcl, settings missingFixes only those (keeps other policy statements), re-checksYes
backend.hcl points at a missing bucket, wrong account or regionStops and says what to fixNo
It never creates a second bucket, never rewrites backend.hcl, never deletes anything, never asks for keys. -WhatIf changes nothing. It replaces about ten console steps.

How to run it

  1. Prerequisites done; section 2d done if your organization restricts regions.
  2. Open Windows PowerShell in the repository root (the folder with scripts and terraform).
  3. Preview with -WhatIf, read the output.
  4. Run without -WhatIf; answer Y if it asks.
# 1. Preview: reads only
.\scripts\bootstrap-state.ps1 -Environment staging -Region us-east-1 -ExpectedAccountId "<account-id>" -WhatIf
# 2. Run: creates or fixes only what is missing
.\scripts\bootstrap-state.ps1 -Environment staging -Region us-east-1 -ExpectedAccountId "<account-id>"

Everything is already applied. Nothing was changed.

<project>-v1-staging-state-<random> for staging" ...

If something goes wrong, or you want to do it by hand
• running scripts is disabled: Set-ExecutionPolicy -Scope CurrentUser RemoteSigned, reopen PowerShell.
• Current AWS account does not match: fix aws configure or the account number.
• Bucket ... named in backend.hcl was not found: fix the name, or move backend.hcl aside to create a new bucket.
• Bootstrap did not finish: inspect the named bucket before retrying.

By hand: S3 (us-east-1) › Create bucket: general purpose, block all public access, versioning on, SSE-S3; then Permissions › Bucket policy with the policy below; then copy backend.example.hcl to backend.hcl with your bucket name. Afterwards run the script with -WhatIf to check your work.

{ "Version": "2012-10-17",
  "Statement": [{ "Sid": "DenyInsecureTransport", "Effect": "Deny", "Principal": "*", "Action": "s3:*",
    "Resource": ["arn:aws:s3:::YOUR-STATE-BUCKET", "arn:aws:s3:::YOUR-STATE-BUCKET/*"],
    "Condition": { "Bool": { "aws:SecureTransport": "false" } } }] }
4 · Build with Terraform

4aFill in site.tfvars ONE TIMEYour PC

WHATYour settings for this environment: region, bucket name, GitHub repository, OIDC provider, alert email.
WHYThe Terraform code is shared; these values make it yours. The file is ignored by Git, so they never get published.
YOU'LL SEEA 6-line file at terraform\environments\staging\site.tfvars.
Check first: if site.tfvars exists, edit it; do not copy the example over it.
Copy-Item .\terraform\environments\staging\site.example.tfvars .\terraform\environments\staging\site.tfvars
SettingValueWatch out
aws_regionus-east-1
environmentstagingMust match the GitHub environment name.
site_bucket_name<project>-staging-site-<timestamp>Globally unique, no underscores, not the state bucket.
github_repository<owner>@<owner-id>/<repo>@<repo-id>GitHub sends numeric IDs for this repo; the plain <owner>/<repo> fails. See below.
github_oidc_provider_arnARN from 2eNot 123456789012, not the role ARN.
alert_emailA mailbox you readNot replace@example.com.
Where to find @<owner-id> and @<repo-id>
  1. Browser: https://api.github.com/repos/<owner>/<repo>: top-level "id" = repo ID; "owner" › "id" = owner ID (public repos).
  2. github.com: repository page, Ctrl+U, then Ctrl+F octolytics-dimension-repository_id and octolytics-dimension-user_id (also private repos you can open).
  3. After a failed deploy: CloudTrail shows the exact subject (see Errors and fixes).
{ "id": **********,   # <repo-id>
  "full_name": "<owner>/<repo>",
  "owner": { "login": "<owner>", "id": ******* },   # <owner-id>
  ... }

4bterraform init Your PC

WHATDownloads the AWS provider plugin and connects Terraform to the state bucket in backend.hcl.
WHYTerraform cannot read or write the state, or talk to AWS, until this is done. Run it once, and again after changing backend.hcl.
CHANGESOnly the local .terraform folder. Nothing in AWS.
Set-Location .\terraform\site
terraform init -reconfigure "-backend-config=..\environments\staging\backend.hcl"
You'll see (real output)

Terraform has been successfully initialized!

Good sign: the two green lines. Bad sign: an error about the bucket or credentials: check backend.hcl and aws sts get-caller-identity.

WHATCompares the code with what exists in AWS and lists exactly what it would create, change or destroy. Saves that list as staging.tfplan.
WHYSo you can review before anything happens. It only reads from AWS.

terraform plan "-var-file=..\environments\staging\site.tfvars" "-out=staging.tfplan"
terraform show staging.tfplan      # optional: read the saved plan again

4fWhat Terraform built, in plain words

ResourceWhat it isWhy it is there
aws_s3_bucket.siteThe website bucketHolds index.html.
..._public_access_block, ..._ownership_controlsBucket locksNo public access, no ACLs: only CloudFront may read.
..._versioning, ..._server_side_encryption_configurationHistory and encryptionOld versions recoverable; files encrypted at rest.
aws_s3_bucket_policy.siteBucket policyLets only this CloudFront distribution read; refuses plain HTTP.
aws_cloudfront_distribution.siteThe CDNGives the HTTPS URL, redirects HTTP to HTTPS, serves index.html.
aws_cloudfront_origin_access_control.siteCloudFront's key to the bucketHow CloudFront proves who it is to S3.
aws_cloudfront_response_headers_policy.siteSecurity headersBrowser protections on every response.
aws_iam_role.deploy + aws_iam_role_policy.deployGitHub's deploy roleOnly this repository's staging environment may use it, and it may only upload index.html.
aws_route53_health_check.siteHealth checkFetches the page over HTTPS every 30 s and looks for the site title.
aws_cloudwatch_metric_alarm.unavailableAlarmGoes to ALARM after 2 failed minutes, back to OK when healthy.
aws_sns_topic.alerts + aws_sns_topic_subscription.alertsAlert emailThe alarm emails you when the site goes down and when it recovers.
5 · Publish with GitHub

5aEnvironment and variables ONE TIMEMANUALGitHub

WHATA GitHub environment named staging, limited to main, holding four variables.
WHYThe deploy workflow reads them to know which role, bucket and URL to use. The AWS role only trusts this environment.
YOU'LL SEE"1 branch and 0 tags allowed" and four variables.
Check first: Settings › Environments. staging exists? Only check the rule and variables. After a new apply, update SITE_BUCKET and WEBSITE_URL: they change on every rebuild.
  1. Push the project to <owner>/<repo> (workflows must be in .github/workflows at the root).
  2. Settings › Environments › New environment › staging › Configure environment.
  3. Deployment branches and tags: Selected branches and tags › Add deployment branch or tag rule › Branch main › Add rule.
  4. Environment variables › Add environment variable for each row:
VariableValue
AWS_REGIONus-east-1
SITE_BUCKEToutput site_bucket_name
WEBSITE_URLoutput website_url, no trailing slash
AWS_ROLE_ARNoutput deploy_role_arn

5bRun the deploy EVERY RELEASEAUTOMATEDGitHub

WHATThe Deploy website workflow signs in to AWS as the deploy role, uploads web/index.html, then fetches the live URL until it matches.
WHYTerraform builds the empty site; this puts the page in it. A push never deploys by itself.
YOU'LL SEEA green run in about 20 seconds, ending with Verified release <commit> at https://d****.cloudfront.net.
  1. Actions tab › Deploy website › Run workflow.
  2. Use workflow from: main, environment staging › green Run workflow.
  3. Open the run; every step turns green. After pushing a fix, start a new run, not Re-run jobs (a re-run reuses the old commit).
6 · After deploy: what you see

6aThe live website EVERY RELEASE

You openYou getMeans
https://d****.cloudfront.net before the first deploy403 ForbiddenNormal: the bucket is still empty.
https://d****.cloudfront.net after the deployThe page below, HTTP 200Live. Cache-Control: no-cache, so a new deploy shows at once.
http://d****.cloudfront.netRedirect to HTTPSCloudFront forces HTTPS.
The S3 bucket URL directly403Good: only CloudFront can read the bucket.

6bAlarm and alert email Workload account, us-east-1

  1. CloudWatch › Alarms › All alarms: <project>-staging-unavailable is OK, a few minutes after the first deploy. Before it, the alarm is In alarm: expected, the page was not there yet.
  2. SNS › Topics › <project>-staging-alerts › Subscriptions: your email is Confirmed. If PendingConfirmation, click the link in the AWS email, or Request confirmation.
  3. From now on, if the page fails for 2 minutes you get an ALARM email, and an OK email when it recovers.
Our run: page HTTP 200 and identical to web/index.html, direct S3 403, alarm OK, email Confirmed. (The stack was destroyed afterwards on 25 Nov 2026, so no screenshots of these pages.)

How we found the real GitHub subject

  1. Workload account, us-east-1: CloudTrail › Event history.
  2. Lookup attribute Event name = AssumeRoleWithWebIdentity; open a failed event.
  3. User name is the exact subject; the part between repo: and :environment: goes into github_repository.

Costs Management account

ItemPrice (AWS price list, us-east-1)
Route 53 health checkHTTPS and text matching: $1.00 each per month (AWS endpoints) or $2.00 each (others); basic check free for the first 50 AWS-endpoint checks, else $0.75.

About $2 to $6 a month while running, covered by the credits. After terraform destroy only the tiny state bucket remains.

Release checklist EVERY RELEASE

  1. Change web/index.html, commit, push to main; wait for Checks to pass.
  2. Infrastructure change (terraform/site/*.tf)? plan, review, apply first (section 4).
  3. Actions › Deploy website › Run workflow › main + staging.
  4. Check the page, the alarm (OK), and that you still get alerts (section 6).

Clean up Your PC

WHATDeletes the 15 site resources, including every file version in the website bucket.
WHYStops all running costs when you no longer need staging.
YOU'LL SEEApply complete! Resources: 0 added, 0 changed, 15 destroyed. and an empty terraform state list.
aws sts get-caller-identity
terraform state list
terraform plan -destroy "-var-file=..\environments\staging\site.tfvars" "-out=staging-destroy.tfplan"
terraform show staging-destroy.tfplan
terraform apply "staging-destroy.tfplan"
Left behind on purpose: the state bucket, the OIDC provider, the SCP entries, the GitHub environment, and the payment method. After a new apply, update SITE_BUCKET and WEBSITE_URL in GitHub.
